agent_explanations_oldest_first.text:
These four wrong answers are reasoning errors, not arithmetic slips, though one also divides 43/4 wrongly. Two problems that fit this description:
- One answer treats a per-item rate as a total ("average of 5 zits each, so S = 5").
- One drops a condition ("after five years").

The other two misread units or a dependency. That is typical of a small model and suggests no single broken component. Before moving to a new mechanism, I'll check where the original model is surprised by correct reasoning, using the token logprobs of the DEV reference solutions from pass 3, which needs no new pass. I'll compare digit tokens that are results of a computation (right after "=") with digit tokens that are operands (quantities chosen from the problem) and with non-digit tokens. If result digits are as well predicted as operands, arithmetic is not the bottleneck and the failures lie in setting up the problem. That would point away from a localisable computation defect. First I'll check how pass 3 is stored.

Pass 3 holds input_ids and token_logprobs for all 1,024 screen texts. I'll read the meta keys and /work/screen_meta.json to find which rows are DEV reference solutions and where each response starts. Then I'll classify reference tokens as result digits (the first digit run after "="), operand digits (other digit runs) or non-digit text, and compare mean logprobs within the response.

The screen meta gives the counts of each text type and the prompt lengths (plens), and the references are the last n_ref texts. I'll check the token_logprobs alignment: whether entry t scores token t given the tokens before it, with entry 0 empty. I'll then compute mean logprob by token class over the response part of the references: digits right after "=", other digits, and non-digits.

Entry t scores token t+1 given the tokens up to t, so a response token at position p has logprob lp[p-1]. First I'll print a short part of one reference response to see the exact format, for example whether the GSM8K calculator annotations <<...>> were kept. The format decides how to classify the "=" results.
